```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

Use `EsgResultFile$fetch_subset()` when you need the original values around a
location for your own interpolation or analysis. On rectilinear latitude and
longitude grids, it reads the enclosing 2x2 neighborhood for the requested
variable and native time window through OPeNDAP. The four corners remain
separate; the acquisition does not interpolate them or download the complete
NetCDF file.

The examples below contact external ESGF services when you run them. They are
shown without execution here, so no live results or connection speeds are
implied. Start with one machine and keep its acquisition directory for resume.

# Describe the Required Data

Each request identifies a location, variable and time window. `request_id`
identifies the demand; the optional `case_id` records which analysis uses it.
Use distinct request IDs when several cases share the same physical data.

```{r requirements}
library(epwshiftr)

requests <- data.frame(
    request_id = "singapore-tas-june-2041",
    case_id = "example-case",
    site_id = "Singapore",
    lon = 103.98,
    lat = 1.37,
    variable_id = "tas",
    time_start = "2041-06-01",
    time_stop = "2041-06-30T23:59:59"
)
dest <- "climate-neighborhoods"
```

Endpoints are inclusive. A date without a time denotes midnight; include a time
to request the whole final day. Dates must be meaningful in the source calendar.
Native CF coordinates are authoritative, including for `360_day` and
`noleap` data; do not infer their calendar dates from a POSIX time proxy.

# Collect the Complete File Directory

Build an explicit query for the model, experiment, member, variable and
frequency you need. Collect every matching File page with `all = TRUE` before
narrowing the result to the requested interval. This searches metadata; it does
not read the climate variable.

```{r collect-files}
query <- esg_query("https://esgf-data.dkrz.de")$activity_id(
    "ScenarioMIP"
)$source_id("MPI-ESM1-2-LR")$experiment_id("ssp126")$variant_label(
    "r1i1p1f1"
)$variable_id("tas")$frequency("mon")$params(table_id = "Amon")

files <- query$collect(type = "File", all = TRUE, limit = FALSE)
files <- files$filter_time(
    requests$time_start,
    requests$time_stop,
    method = "drs"
)
candidates <- files$access_plan()
attr(candidates, "directory_complete")
```

`access_plan()` lists compatible OPeNDAP Replica candidates. Successful data
reads cannot establish that missing query pages were collected. The separate
`directory_complete` flag records that distinction; filtering or deliberately
slicing an already complete directory retains its directory evidence.

# Acquire the Four Corners

```{r acquire}
result <- files$fetch_subset(
    requests,
    dest,
    workers = 4L,
    node_workers = 2L,
    timeout = 180,
    retries = 2L,
    network_id = "single-machine"
)
result$directory_complete
result$complete
subset_status(dest, "nodes")
```

The package switches to another compatible Replica after a read failure and
updates node ranking from actual demand reads. It does not require a separate
speed test of every candidate. A file whose candidates fail releases its worker
so other files can continue; `retries` bounds later attempts. Node observations
belong to the current client and `network_id`, so another machine can have a
different ranking.

`result$complete` concerns native coverage of the selected Files.
`result$directory_complete` concerns File-query pagination. Neither establishes
that every variable, frequency, model or year required by your study is present.
Check those study requirements separately. A case label is an association, not a
scientific acceptance rule.

# Inspect Saved Values and Gaps

After an acquisition call returns, inspect its local results:

```{r local-results}
subset_status(dest)
subset_status(dest, "attempts")
raw <- read_subset(dest, case_id = "example-case")
head(raw$values)
head(raw$neighborhoods)
raw$gaps$directory
raw$gaps$unmatched
raw$gaps$incomplete_requests
raw$gaps$invalid_blocks
```

`raw$values` contains unique native point/time values with their coordinates and
CF time information. `raw$neighborhoods` relates them to each location's corners
and requested window; `raw$links` retains the case/request associations. Keep
these together when comparing interpolation algorithms.

`subset_status()` and `read_subset()` use local data only. Directory gaps,
unmatched requests, missing native coverage and invalid saved blocks remain
explicit; the reader does not fill them through hidden network access.

# Resume in the Same Directory

Repeat the acquisition with the same requests and destination:

```{r resume}
resumed <- files$fetch_subset(
    requests,
    dest,
    resume = TRUE,
    workers = 4L,
    network_id = "single-machine"
)
raw <- read_subset(dest, case_id = "example-case")
raw$gaps$incomplete_requests
```

Verified saved blocks are reused and only outstanding demand is read. A fully
saved request does not need another climate-data read. With the default
`discover = TRUE`, an original, unsliced partial File query automatically collects
its missing pages and saves the completed directory for local reuse on repeat
calls. An explicitly sliced result is never expanded automatically, even when
it contains every held row. Existing directory gaps remain visible when
collection context is unknown or discovery is disabled. To resolve a partial
original directory, explicitly collect the original File query with `all = TRUE`
and supply that complete result to `fetch_subset()`.

Keep one writer per acquisition directory. If work is later divided between
machines, give each machine a fixed File list and its own destination, and
retain the request/case associations when combining results.

See [Work with ESGF Query Results](esgf-query-results.html) for query selection,
and [Troubleshoot ESGF Workflows](esgf-troubleshooting.html) for access failures.
